name: June 2019 Endline Grant Updated Version of NI CEA Early 2018 (with new baseline rates)
summary: Gives caregivers small cash incentives to bring infants for routine vaccinations in northern Nigeria (2019 endline grant). GiveWell's spreadsheet "June 2019 Endline Grant Updated Version of NI CEA Early 2018 (with new baseline rates)", linked from its grant page. Every number is traced from the sheet's bottom line; calculated rows reproduce the sheet's own values.

rows.explainer: From SAGE 2014 Pertussis Report, p. 18: "Based on this in April 2014 SAGE concluded that there is increasing and consistent evidence  both from observational and analytical studies from a number of industrialized countries  using aP and wP to show that a single dose of either pertussis vaccine in infancy has around 50% effectiveness in preventing severe disease, hospitalization, and death and that 2 doses  of either pertussis vaccine offers higher protection (83%-87%)." (p. 413) Yearly susceptibility of 30% is consistent with prevaccination-era epidimiology of high-transmission airborn diseases like measles. rows.explainer: Guess. We have not found good evidence about the case fatality of severe rotavirus disease. We have found some observational studies of children admitted with rotavirus to health facilities: (1) a tertiary health facility in the Gambia. Case fatality for rotavirus was 4.5%, with 111 rotavirus-positive cases. (Ideh et al. 2011, p. 61.) We expect that case fatality in a general population (who may or may not access a health facility) is notably higher. (2) In Guinea-Bissau, hospital surveillance found case-fatality of 8%. (Rodrigues et al. 2007, p. 233.) We are aware of Tate et al. 2016, estimates of rotavirus mortality. For comparison, note that we estimate the case fatality rate of measles in Nigeria at 4-5%.

rows.explainer: The 2016 national SIA in Nigeria included a coverage survey finding 84% coverage. See the "Retrospective Summary of Measles SIAs" excel file linked to at the bottom of the WHO immunization surveillance front page. While we place higher confidence in SIA coverage surveys than in routinely reported SIA coverage, we remain not confident in the accuracy of SIA coverage surveys. rows.label: SIA vaccine efficacy
rows.explainer: Measles vaccination given at a later age (after 12-18 months) is more effacacious than vaccination given at 9 months. Uzicanin and Zimmerman 2011, a review of vaccine efficacy studies published in 1960-2010, estimate vaccine efficacy over 12mo at 88% for the WHO Africa region, based on 4 point estimates of field effectiveness. (Table 2, p. S145) We are also aware of Demicheli et al. 2012, a Cochrane review of MMR vaccine effectiveness based on three cohort studies, which concludes that "Based on the available evidence, one MMR vaccine dose is at least 95% effective in preventing clinical measles" (p. 1). Measles vaccination is generall considered highly effective (~95%); however, we are moved by considerations that field effectiveness in African contexts may be lower (e.g. due to vaccine distribution challenges, cold chain, expiry).

rows.label: SIA vaccine efficacy
rows.explainer: Measles vaccination given at a later age (after 12-18 months) is more effacacious than vaccination given at 9 months. Uzicanin and Zimmerman 2011, a review of vaccine efficacy studies published in 1960-2010, estimate vaccine efficacy over 12mo at 88% for the WHO Africa region, based on 4 point estimates of field effectiveness. (Table 2, p. S145) We are also aware of Demicheli et al. 2012, a Cochrane review of MMR vaccine effectiveness based on three cohort studies, which concludes that "Based on the available evidence, one MMR vaccine dose is at least 95% effective in preventing clinical measles" (p. 1). Measles vaccination is generall considered highly effective (~95%); however, we are moved by considerations that field effectiveness in African contexts may be lower (e.g. due to vaccine distribution challenges, cold chain, expiry). https://academic.oup.com/jid/article/204/suppl_1/S133/2

rows.explainer: Cutts et al. 2005, an RCT of PCV efficacy in the Gambia found a 16% (per-protocol) reduction in all-cause mortality in infants under 30mo treated with 3 doses of PCV compared to placebo. rows.explainer: Guess. We have not found good evidence about the case fatality of severe rotavirus disease. We have found some observational studies of children admitted with rotavirus to health facilities: (1) a tertiary health facility in the Gambia. Case fatality for rotavirus was 4.5%, with 111 rotavirus-positive cases. (Ideh et al. 2011, p. 61.) For comparison, note that we estimate the case fatality rate of measles in Nigeria at 4-5%. http://www.ajol.info/index.php/abs/article/view/69203 http://journals.lww.com/pidj/Abstract/2007/03000/Hospital_Surveillance_of_Rotavirus_Infection_and.8.aspx

New Incentives believes that it can get higher exchange rates but needs to make projections based on the minimum rate it can likely receive. This has implications on the CEA model. Wolfson et al. 2009 (Table 2, p. 202), as updated by Simons et al. 2012 (Supplementary appendix, Table 3, p. 4) provides estimates (based on expert panel) of measles case fatality by country and categorizes Nigeria in the 4%-5% CFR range. Additional considerations: We believe that the North West zone of Nigeria is likely to have weaker health infrastructure and higher mortality rates than the country as a whole. We know that the population reached by New Incentives has some degree of clinic access. We expect that measles CFR is notably higher during outbreaks: We note Nandy et al. 2006, which found measles CFR of 9.7% in a sample affected by a 2003 outbreak in eastern Niger (near North West Nigeria). We note Grais et al. 2007, which found a measles CFR of 10.8% in Dong District, Adamawa State Nigeria, during an outbreak in 2004-2005. https://academic.oup.com/ije/article/38/1/192/696766/E

rows.explainer: The 2016 national SIA in Nigeria included a coverage survey finding 84% coverage. See the "Retrospective Summary of Measles SIAs" excel file linked to at the bottom of the WHO immunization surveillance front page. While we place higher confidence in SIA coverage surveys than in routinely reported SIA coverage, we remain not confident in the accuracy of SIA coverage surveys. We suspect that SIA coverage varies by region and might be much lower in areas where New Incentives works, and in particular in the North West. We have arbitrarily reduced the survey-reported coverage estimate in response to our expectations. http://www.who.int/immunization/monitoring_surveillance/data/en/

rows.label: SIA vaccine efficacy
rows.explainer: Measles vaccination given at a later age (after 12-18 months) is more effacacious than vaccination given at 9 months. Uzicanin and Zimmerman 2011, a review of vaccine efficacy studies published in 1960-2010, estimate vaccine efficacy over 12mo at 88% for the WHO Africa region, based on 4 point estimates of field effectiveness. (Table 2, p. S145) We are also aware of Demicheli et al. 2012, a Cochrane review of MMR vaccine effectiveness based on three cohort studies, which concludes that "Based on the available evidence, one MMR vaccine dose is at least 95% effective in preventing clinical measles" (p. 1). Measles vaccination is generall considered highly effective (~95%); however, we are moved by considerations that field effectiveness in African contexts may be lower (e.g. due to vaccine distribution challenges, cold chain, expiry). https://academic.oup.com/jid/article/204/suppl_1/S133/2

rows.explainer: Crowcroft et al. 2003 estimate case-fatality in high-mortality countries at 3.7% for infants and 1% for children 1-4 years of age, noting that "For countries with high child mortality published material is extremely limited, with only six studies meeting quality criteria. rows.explainer: Cutts et al. 2005, an RCT of PCV efficacy in the Gambia found a 16% (per-protocol) reduction in all-cause mortality in infants under 30mo treated with 3 doses of PCV compared to placebo. We have not examined this study closely. We have not conducted a review searching for other evidence of PCV effectiveness. rows.label: SIA vaccine efficacy
rows.explainer: Measles vaccination given at a later age (after 12-18 months) is more effacacious than vaccination given at 9 months. Uzicanin and Zimmerman 2011, a review of vaccine efficacy studies published in 1960-2010, estimate vaccine efficacy over 12mo at 88% for the WHO Africa region, based on 4 point estimates of field effectiveness. (Table 2, p. S145) We are also aware of Demicheli et al. 2012, a Cochrane review of MMR vaccine effectiveness based on three cohort studies, which concludes that "Based on the available evidence, one MMR vaccine dose is at least 95% effective in preventing clinical measles" (p. 1). Measles vaccination is generall considered highly effective (~95%); however, we are moved by considerations that field effectiveness in African contexts may be lower (e.g. due to vaccine distribution challenges, cold chain, expiry). https://academic.oup.com/jid/article/204/suppl_1/S133/2

Tuberculosis: Chance of infection if susceptible, yearly (2020)
rows.explainer: Trunz, Fine and Dye 2006, a meta-analysis and modeling study. This paper presents estimated annual chance of infection in several countries in east Africa (p. 1174) based on review of tuberculin surveys in children: 0.9 and 0.68 in Tanzania, 1.0 in Malawi, 1.1 in Kenya, 1.2 in Madagascar. The authors estimate annual chance of infection at 0.13-1.95 in Africa (low HIV) contexts, and 0.57-2.16 in Africa (high HIV) contexts. Believing that HIV prevalence in Nigeria is middling (https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/the-world-factbook/rankorder/2155rank.html), we take the middle of the entire range for our estimate of annual chance of infection in Nigeria. This is the chance of contracting tuberculosis; the chance of progression to active tuberculosis and death is represented in the case fatality rate. http://www.thelancet.com/pdfs/journals/lancet/PIIS0140-6736(06)68507-3.pdf

Efficacy of 3 doses of PCV against all-cause mortality
rows.explainer: Cutts et al. 2005, an RCT of PCV efficacy in the Gambia found a 16% (per-protocol) reduction in all-cause mortality in infants under 30mo treated with 3 doses of PCV compared to placebo. See Table 5, p. 1144. This study was not designed to be powered to find a significant effect on mortality, but regardless found a barely-significant effect on mortality. We have not examined this study closely. We have not conducted a review searching for other evidence of PCV effectiveness. Cutts et al. 2005 is the source of efficacy evidence cited (p. 391) by Sinha et al. 2007, a cost-effectiveness analysis of adding PCV to the immunization schedule in Gavi-eligible countries. http://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(05)71876-6/abstract https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17276779

rows.explainer: Guess. We have not found good evidence about the case fatality of severe rotavirus disease. We have found some observational studies of children admitted with rotavirus to health facilities: (1) a tertiary health facility in the Gambia. rows.label: SIA vaccine efficacy
rows.explainer: Measles vaccination given at a later age (after 12-18 months) is more effacacious than vaccination given at 9 months. Uzicanin and Zimmerman 2011, a review of vaccine efficacy studies published in 1960-2010, estimate vaccine efficacy over 12mo at 88% for the WHO Africa region, based on 4 point estimates of field effectiveness. (Table 2, p. S145) We are also aware of Demicheli et al. 2012, a Cochrane review of MMR vaccine effectiveness based on three cohort studies, which concludes that "Based on the available evidence, one MMR vaccine dose is at least 95% effective in preventing clinical measles" (p. 1). Measles vaccination is generall considered highly effective (~95%); however, we are moved by considerations that field effectiveness in African contexts may be lower (e.g. due to vaccine distribution challenges, cold chain, expiry). https://academic.oup.com/jid/article/204/suppl_1/S133/2

rows.explainer: Cutts et al. 2005, an RCT of PCV efficacy in the Gambia found a 16% (per-protocol) reduction in all-cause mortality in infants under 30mo treated with 3 doses of PCV compared to placebo. See Table 5, p. 1144. This study was not designed to be powered to find a significant effect on mortality, but regardless found a barely-significant effect on mortality. We have not examined this study closely. We have not conducted a review searching for other evidence of PCV effectiveness. Cutts et al. 2005 is the source of efficacy evidence cited (p. 391) by Sinha et al. 2007, a cost-effectiveness analysis of adding PCV to the immunization schedule in Gavi-eligible countries. http://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(05)71876-6/abstract https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17276779

rows.explainer: Guess. We have not found good evidence about the case fatality of severe rotavirus disease. rows.label: SIA vaccine efficacy
rows.explainer: Measles vaccination given at a later age (after 12-18 months) is more effacacious than vaccination given at 9 months. Uzicanin and Zimmerman 2011, a review of vaccine efficacy studies published in 1960-2010, estimate vaccine efficacy over 12mo at 88% for the WHO Africa region, based on 4 point estimates of field effectiveness. (Table 2, p. S145) We are also aware of Demicheli et al. 2012, a Cochrane review of MMR vaccine effectiveness based on three cohort studies, which concludes that "Based on the available evidence, one MMR vaccine dose is at least 95% effective in preventing clinical measles" (p. 1). Measles vaccination is generall considered highly effective (~95%); however, we are moved by considerations that field effectiveness in African contexts may be lower (e.g. due to vaccine distribution challenges, cold chain, expiry). https://academic.oup.com/jid/article/204/suppl_1/S133/2

rows.explainer: Cutts et al. 2005, an RCT of PCV efficacy in the Gambia found a 16% (per-protocol) reduction in all-cause mortality in infants under 30mo treated with 3 doses of PCV compared to placebo. See Table 5, p. 1144. This study was not designed to be powered to find a significant effect on mortality, but regardless found a barely-significant effect on mortality. We have not examined this study closely. We have not conducted a review searching for other evidence of PCV effectiveness. Cutts et al. 2005 is the source of efficacy evidence cited (p. 391) by Sinha et al. 2007, a cost-effectiveness analysis of adding PCV to the immunization schedule in Gavi-eligible countries. http://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(05)71876-6/abstract https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17276779

rows.explainer: Guess. We have not found good evidence about the case fatality of severe rotavirus disease. rows.label: SIA vaccine efficacy
rows.explainer: Measles vaccination given at a later age (after 12-18 months) is more effacacious than vaccination given at 9 months. Uzicanin and Zimmerman 2011, a review of vaccine efficacy studies published in 1960-2010, estimate vaccine efficacy over 12mo at 88% for the WHO Africa region, based on 4 point estimates of field effectiveness. (Table 2, p. S145) We are also aware of Demicheli et al. 2012, a Cochrane review of MMR vaccine effectiveness based on three cohort studies, which concludes that "Based on the available evidence, one MMR vaccine dose is at least 95% effective in preventing clinical measles" (p. 1). Measles vaccination is generall considered highly effective (~95%); however, we are moved by considerations that field effectiveness in African contexts may be lower (e.g. due to vaccine distribution challenges, cold chain, expiry). https://academic.oup.com/jid/article/204/suppl_1/S133/2

rows.explainer: Crowcroft et al. 2003 estimate case-fatality in high-mortality countries at 3.7% for infants and 1% for children 1-4 years of age, noting that "For countries with high child mortality published material is extremely limited, with only six studies meeting quality criteria. (p. 414) Datta et al. 2012 describe that "A large outbreak of pertussis was detected during March 2011 in Goilala, a remote district of the Central Province in Papua New Guinea, characterized by rugged topography with no road access from the provincial headquarters... There were 205 suspected pertussis cases, with a case-fatality rate (CFR) of 3%." (p. 3) http://www.thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473-3099(03)00669-8/abstract http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
